data.title: How a Bicycle Moves
data.subtitle: Discover the mechanical journey from your feet to the street
data.overview: Every time you hop on a bicycle and push your feet down, an invisible chain reaction of gears and wheels turns your leg power into fast forward motion.

steps.title: Stepping on the Levers
steps.description: Your foot applies downward force against a metal platform attached to a central arm. This direct pressure forces the arm to rotate in a wide circle.
steps.imagePrompt: Close-up of a child's sneakers pushing down on a metal bicycle pedal, photographed outdoors on a paved sidewalk in bright afternoon sunlight.
steps.whatsHappening: Your muscles contract to push the pedal downward, creating rotational force called torque.
steps.funFact: Your leg muscles can produce up to 100 watts of power during a casual ride.
steps.purpose: It starts the rotational movement that the rest of the bicycle passes along to the wheel.

steps.title: Spinning the Metal Wheel
steps.description: The rotating arm turns a large metal circle with teeth on its outer edge. This toothed circle is firmly attached to the frame near the center of the bicycle.
steps.imagePrompt: Side view of a bicycle chainring and metal crank arm on a modern mountain bike, captured in natural shade with visible metallic textures.
steps.whatsHappening: The crank arms act as extensions of your legs, magnifying the distance your feet travel.
steps.purpose: It gathers the circular force from your legs and prepares to share it with the back wheel.

steps.title: Pulling the Metal Links
steps.description: As the large toothed circle turns, it catches the individual metal loops of a continuous chain. These tiny interconnected links loop tightly all the way back to the rear wheel.
steps.imagePrompt: Close-up photograph of a metal bicycle chain resting on shiny gear teeth, shot outside with natural daylight highlighting the oily steel links.
steps.funFact: A standard bicycle chain has over 100 individual moving links working together.
steps.purpose: It transfers the turning energy from the middle of the frame all the way to the back axle.

steps.title: Turning the Rear Cogs
steps.description: The moving chain snags onto a much smaller cluster of toothed wheels attached directly to the center of the back tire. Because this back wheel is smaller, it spins much faster than the front pedals.
steps.imagePrompt: Macro photo of a bicycle cassette gear cluster and derailleur on a parked road bike, illuminated by soft daylight.
steps.whatsHappening: Passing force from a large gear to a small gear increases rotational speed.
steps.purpose: It multiplies your speed so the bicycle travels much faster than your feet are moving.

steps.title: Rolling Across the Ground
steps.description: The spinning back tire grips the pavement and pushes backward against the Earth. According to the laws of physics, this friction pushes the entire bicycle forward into a smooth glide.
steps.imagePrompt: Low angle shot of a rubber bicycle tire rolling over asphalt on a sunny day, focusing on the tread pattern and road texture.
steps.funFact: Good tire tread can grip the road even when tiny water droplets coat the pavement.
steps.purpose: It translates internal mechanical spinning into real world travel across the neighborhood.

summary.text: By connecting your leg muscles through pedals, chains, and gears, a bicycle multiplies your strength to roll smoothly across the pavement.
summary.keyTakeaway: Gears of different sizes let you trade raw strength for incredible speed.

quickFacts.whereItHappens: Along the bicycle frame from pedals to tires
